points.text: The moles of one component divided by the total moles of all the components.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Raoult’s law

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Henry’s law
text: Define Henry’s law.

points.text: At constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above it.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:an azeotrope
text: Define an azeotrope.

points.text: A liquid mixture that boils at a constant temperature, with the vapour having the same composition as the liquid.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:an azeotrope
text: State what is meant by an azeotrope, and add one further point about it.

points.text: A liquid mixture that boils at a constant temperature, with the vapour having the same composition as the liquid.
It can’t be separated by simple distillation.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:osmosis
text: Define osmosis.

points.text: The flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane, from the dilute solution to the concentrated one.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:colligative properties
text: Define colligative properties.

points.text: Properties that depend on the number of solute particles, not on their nature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:an ideal solution
text: Define an ideal solution.

points.text: A solution that obeys Raoult’s law at every composition, with no heat or volume change on mixing.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a solution
text: Define a solution.

points.text: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances, whose composition can vary within limits.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a solute
text: Define a solute.

points.text: The component of a solution present in the smaller amount, usually.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a solvent
text: Define a solvent.

points.text: The component of a solution present in the larger amount, usually, which decides its physical state.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:solubility
text: Define solubility.

points.text: The largest amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a saturated solution
text: Define a saturated solution.

points.text: A solution in equilibrium with undissolved solute, which can’t dissolve more at that temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:normality
text: Define normality.

points.text: The number of gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:mass percentage
text: Define mass percentage.

points.text: The mass of a component per 100 parts of the mass of the solution.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:parts per million
text: Define parts per million.

points.text: The number of parts of a component per million parts of the whole solution.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a solid solution
text: Define a solid solution.

points.text: A homogeneous mixture in which the solvent is solid, as in an alloy.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:vapour pressure
text: Define vapour pressure.

points.text: The pressure of a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:relative lowering of vapour pressure
text: Define relative lowering of vapour pressure.

points.text: The fall in vapour pressure of a solvent divided by the vapour pressure of the pure solvent.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:elevation of boiling point
text: Define elevation of boiling point.

points.text: The rise in the boiling point of a solvent when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:depression of freezing point
text: Define depression of freezing point.

points.text: The fall in the freezing point of a solvent when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:the molal elevation constant
text: Define the molal elevation constant.

points.text: The rise in boiling point of a solvent for a 1 molal solution of a non-volatile, unassociated solute.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:the molal depression constant
text: Define the molal depression constant.

points.text: The fall in freezing point of a solvent for a 1 molal solution of a non-volatile, unassociated solute.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:osmotic pressure
text: Define osmotic pressure.

points.text: The extra pressure needed on a solution to stop the flow of solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a semipermeable membrane
text: Define a semipermeable membrane.

points.text: A membrane that lets solvent molecules pass through it, but not solute particles.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:isotonic solutions
text: Define isotonic solutions.

points.text: Solutions with the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:a hypertonic solution
text: Define a hypertonic solution.

points.text: A solution with a higher osmotic pressure than another solution.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:the van’t Hoff factor
text: Define the van’t Hoff factor.

points.text: The ratio of the observed colligative property to the calculated one, which accounts for association or dissociation.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:association of a solute
text: Define association of a solute.

points.text: The joining of two or more solute particles into one, which lowers the number of particles in solution.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:dissociation of a solute
text: Define dissociation of a solute.

points.text: The splitting of a solute into ions, which raises the number of particles in solution.

facts: c12-1a:Fish find it harder to breathe in warm water.
text: Give a reason: Fish find it harder to breathe in warm water.

points.text: Less oxygen dissolves in water at higher temperatures.
Henry’s constant rises with temperature, so solubility falls.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Salt is spread on icy roads.
text: Give a reason: Salt is spread on icy roads.

points.text: Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water.
So ice melts at temperatures below 0 °C.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:A cucumber shrinks in salty water.
text: Give a reason: A cucumber shrinks in salty water.

points.text: The salt solution is hypertonic to the cucumber’s cells.
So water leaves the cells by osmosis.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Soft drink bottles are sealed under high pressure.
text: Give a reason: Soft drink bottles are sealed under high pressure.

points.text: A high pressure of CO₂ raises its solubility, by Henry’s law.
Opening the bottle lowers the pressure, so the gas comes out.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:The boiling point of a solution of a non-volatile solute is higher than that of
text: Give a reason: The boiling point of a solution of a non-volatile solute is higher than that of the solvent.

points.text: The solute lowers the vapour pressure.
So a higher temperature is needed for it to reach atmospheric pressure.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Molality is preferred over molarity in work over a range of temperatures.
text: Give a reason: Molality is preferred over molarity in work over a range of temperatures.

points.text: Molality uses mass of solvent, which doesn’t change with temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Ethylene glycol is added to a car’s radiator in winter.
text: Give a reason: Ethylene glycol is added to a car’s radiator in winter.

points.text: It lowers the freezing point of the water and stops it freezing in the engine.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:A 0.1 M solution of urea and a 0.1 M solution of glucose are isotonic.
text: Give a reason: A 0.1 M solution of urea and a 0.1 M solution of glucose are isotonic.

points.text: Neither dissociates nor associates, so both have the same number of particles per litre.
So, at the same temperature, they have the same osmotic pressure, π = CRT.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its solvent.
text: Give a reason: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its solvent.

points.text: Its vapour pressure is lowered, so it matches that of the solid only at a lower temperature.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Eating too much salt can cause swelling of the body.
text: Give a reason: Eating too much salt can cause swelling of the body.

points.text: Water is held back in the tissue cells by osmosis.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Meat is preserved by salting.
text: Give a reason: Meat is preserved by salting.

points.text: Bacteria on it lose water by osmosis, so they shrivel and die.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Fruit is preserved by adding a lot of sugar.
text: Give a reason: Fruit is preserved by adding a lot of sugar.

points.text: Bacteria on it lose water by osmosis, and so they can’t grow.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Plants take in water through their roots.
text: Give a reason: Plants take in water through their roots.

points.text: The cell sap inside root cells has a higher concentration than the soil’s water.
So water enters by osmosis.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Intravenous injections must be isotonic with blood.
text: Give a reason: Intravenous injections must be isotonic with blood.

points.text: A hypertonic fluid would make cells lose water and shrink.
A hypotonic one would make them swell and burst.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Osmotic pressure is better than other properties for finding the molar mass of a
text: Give a reason: Osmotic pressure is better than other properties for finding the molar mass of a polymer.

points.text: It is large even for a very dilute solution.
It is measured at room temperature, so a protein isn’t damaged.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:NaCl has about twice the expected depression of freezing point.
text: Give a reason: NaCl has about twice the expected depression of freezing point.

points.text: It splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so there are nearly twice as many particles.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Acetic acid in benzene shows about half the expected freezing-point depression.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:A non-ideal mixture of chloroform and acetone has a lower vapour pressure than e
text: Give a reason: A non-ideal mixture of chloroform and acetone has a lower vapour pressure than expected.

points.text: Hydrogen bonds form between its two components, which reduces their escape into vapour.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Ethanol and water can’t be fully separated by fractional distillation.
text: Give a reason: Ethanol and water can’t be fully separated by fractional distillation.

points.text: They form an azeotrope of about 95% ethanol, which boils at a fixed composition.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Gas bubbles form in a bottle of soda when it is opened.
text: Give a reason: Gas bubbles form in a bottle of soda when it is opened.

points.text: The pressure falls, so by Henry’s law the gas’s solubility falls.
The extra gas escapes as bubbles.

subject: chemistry
facts: c12-1a:Mountaineers use oxygen cylinders at high altitudes.
text: Give a reason: Mountaineers use oxygen cylinders at high altitudes.

points.text: The partial pressure of oxygen is low there, so less of it dissolves in the blood.

points.text: By Raoult’s law, P = x₁P⁰.
So P⁰ − P = P⁰(1 − x₁) = P⁰x₂.

why: The molality varies in inverse proportion to the mass of solvent, and the molality varies in direct proportion to the amount of solute, so the factor is $2^{-1} \times 0.5^{1}$ = 0.25. The other options come from common slips: 1 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 4 if you turned the ratio upside down; 0.5 if you changed only the mass of solvent.

text: A class studies a sugar solution in a school project. Situation: Molarity. The volume of solution is doubled and the amount of solute is tripled. By what factor does the molarity change?
why: The molarity varies in inverse proportion to the volume of solution, and the molarity varies in direct proportion to the amount of solute, so the factor is $2^{-1} \times 3^{1}$ = 1.5. The other options come from common slips: 6 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 0.667 if you turned the ratio upside down; 0.5 if you changed only the volume of solution.

text: A workshop mixes antifreeze for a radiator. Situation: Elevation of boiling point. The molality is doubled and the ebullioscopic constant is tripled. By what factor does the elevation of boiling point change?
why: The elevation of boiling point varies in direct proportion to the molality, and the elevation of boiling point varies in direct proportion to the ebullioscopic constant, so the factor is $2^{1} \times 3^{1}$ = 6. The other options come from common slips: 0.167 if you turned the ratio upside down; 2 if you changed only the molality; 3 if you changed only the ebullioscopic constant.

text: A student measures a solution’s vapour pressure in the lab. Situation: Molar mass from depression of freezing point. The cryoscopic constant is tripled and the mass of solvent is reduced to a quarter, with everything else kept the same. By what factor does the molar mass of solute change?
